rooms.about: This year you will read fiction, poetry, drama and nonfiction closely, cite strong evidence, and analyze how authors build meaning. You will write arguments, informative essays and narratives, sharpen grammar, and practice research and speaking skills.

units.t: Close Reading and Citing Strong Evidence
learn: Close reading means reading a passage more than once, slowly, with a question in mind. The first read is for the general idea; later reads look at word choice, structure and details that support a deeper meaning.
An inference is a logical conclusion based on evidence plus what you already know. Strong evidence is a quotation or detail that directly supports your claim, not one that only loosely relates to it.

When you cite evidence, introduce it, quote it exactly, and explain it. A useful pattern is claim, evidence, reasoning: say what you think, show the words from the text, then explain how those words prove your point.
Eighth graders are expected to choose the evidence that most strongly supports an analysis. If two quotations could work, pick the one that leaves the least room for another interpretation.
units.try: Pick a short story you have read. Write one claim about the main character, such as “Maya is more afraid than she admits.” Find two quotations that could support it. Write two sentences for each, explaining how the exact words prove your claim, then decide which quotation is stronger and why.
check: A logical conclusion based on evidence and prior knowledge
A direct quotation copied from the text
A summary of the plot in order
In claim, evidence, reasoning, what does the reasoning do?
Explains how the evidence proves the claim
Restates the title of the text

learn: A theme is a message about life or people that a text develops, such as “courage can mean admitting fear.” A topic is one word, like courage; a theme is a full statement about that topic.

Themes are developed over the whole text through characters’ choices, conflicts, setting and the way things turn out. Track how a character changes from beginning to end; the change often points to the theme.
An objective summary tells the main events or ideas in your own words without opinions. It is shorter than the original, keeps the order clear, and leaves out minor details and personal reactions.
A strong summary of a story usually names the main character, the central conflict, the key turning point and the resolution, in about five to eight sentences.
units.try: Retell a well-known fable in no more than five sentences without using the words “I think” or any opinion. Then write one sentence stating its theme as a complete thought, not a single word.
check: Which is a theme rather than a topic?
Honesty builds trust that is hard to rebuild once broken
What does an objective summary leave out?

learn: Authors reveal characters through what they say, do, think and how others react to them. Dialogue can show personality, reveal conflict and push the plot forward in a single line.

An incident is a specific event. Analyzing how an incident moves the plot means asking: what changes because of this moment? Often a key incident forces a decision that reveals who a character really is.
Dramatic irony happens when readers know something a character does not. It creates suspense or humor, because we watch characters make choices we know are mistakes.
Point of view also matters. A first-person narrator may be unreliable, meaning their version of events is limited or biased, so readers must look for clues that suggest a different truth.
units.try: Write a short scene of six to ten lines of dialogue between two friends where one is hiding a secret. Let the reader learn the secret through a clue the other friend misses. Label where the dramatic irony begins.
check: When the reader knows something a character does not
When a character tells a joke
When the story is set in the past
An unreliable narrator is one whose account is
Limited or biased, so it may not be fully true

units.t: Word Choice, Tone and Figurative Language
learn: Connotation is the feeling a word carries beyond its dictionary meaning. “Thrifty” and “cheap” both mean careful with money, but thrifty sounds positive and cheap sounds negative.
Tone is the author’s attitude, shown through word choice. Tones can be hopeful, bitter, playful, solemn or sarcastic. Mood is how the reader feels, such as tense or peaceful.

Figurative language includes simile (comparison using like or as), metaphor (direct comparison), personification (human traits given to things), hyperbole (exaggeration) and allusion (a reference to a famous work, person or event).
Analogies compare relationships, such as “a key is to a lock as a password is to an account.” Writers use them to explain hard ideas by linking them to familiar ones.
units.try: Rewrite this sentence three times, each with a different tone (cheerful, gloomy, sarcastic) by changing only the word choice: “The class went on a field trip to the museum.” Underline the words that create each tone.
check: The feeling or association a word carries
The dictionary definition of a word
The number of syllables in a word
“The wind whispered through the trees” is an example of

learn: Poems are built from lines and stanzas. Structure matters: a sonnet has 14 lines, a haiku traditionally has three lines of 5, 7 and 5 syllables, and free verse has no fixed rhyme or rhythm.

Sound devices add music. Alliteration repeats beginning consonant sounds, assonance repeats vowel sounds, and onomatopoeia uses words that imitate sounds, like buzz or crack. Rhyme scheme is labeled with letters, such as ABAB.
Meter is the pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables. Iambic pentameter has five pairs per line, each da-DUM, and is common in older English poetry.
To analyze a poem, read it aloud twice, note the speaker and situation, mark images and sound devices, then ask how the form supports the meaning, such as a short line creating a sudden pause.
units.try: Write a four-line poem about your morning with an ABAB rhyme scheme and at least one example of alliteration. Read it aloud and tap the beat of each line to hear its rhythm.
check: How many lines are in a sonnet?
Repeating the first consonant sound, as in “silver snakes slide,” is called

units.t: Drama and Comparing Texts Across Forms
learn: A play is written to be performed. It uses a cast list, acts and scenes, dialogue and stage directions, which are notes in italics or brackets that tell actors how to move or speak.

A monologue is a long speech by one character to others; a soliloquy is spoken alone so the audience hears the character’s private thoughts; an aside is a short comment to the audience that other characters do not hear.
When a story becomes a film or stage version, directors make choices. Comparing versions means asking what was kept, cut or changed, and how those choices affect the meaning or mood.
Modern stories often borrow from older ones, such as myths or religious stories. Noticing these patterns, called archetypes, like the hero’s journey, helps you see how writers make old material new.
units.try: Choose a short scene from a story you know and rewrite it as a script with character names, dialogue and at least three stage directions in brackets. Then read it aloud with a family member.
check: A speech a character makes alone on stage to reveal thoughts is a
What do stage directions tell actors?
How to move, speak or where to be

learn: Informational texts explain or inform. Authors organize them with structures such as cause and effect, problem and solution, compare and contrast, and chronological order. Signal words like because, however and as a result show the structure.
A central idea is the main point the author develops. Find it by asking what most of the paragraphs have in common, then trace how each section adds to it.

When evaluating an argument, identify the claim, then judge whether the reasons are sound and the evidence is relevant and sufficient. Watch for irrelevant evidence that sounds good but does not prove the claim.
Authors may acknowledge conflicting viewpoints. Strong writers respond to opposing views fairly instead of ignoring them or attacking the people who hold them.
units.try: Find a short opinion article meant for students in a school newspaper or textbook. Write down the claim, list each reason, and mark each piece of evidence as relevant or irrelevant. Decide whether the evidence is enough to convince you.
check: Signal words like “as a result” usually show which structure?
Evidence that sounds convincing but does not support the claim is

learn: An argument essay states a clear claim and supports it with logical reasons and credible evidence. The introduction gives context and ends with the claim, often as a thesis statement.
A counterclaim is an opposing view. Eighth graders acknowledge it and then rebut it, explaining why the claim still holds. Phrases like “Some people argue… however…” help.
Use transitions to connect ideas: furthermore, in contrast, for example, therefore. Keep a formal style, avoiding slang and phrases like “I feel like.”
The conclusion restates the claim in new words and shows why it matters. A good conclusion does not simply repeat the introduction; it leaves the reader with a reason to care.
units.try: Write a one-paragraph argument answering “Should middle schools start later in the morning?” Include a claim, two reasons with evidence or examples, one counterclaim with a rebuttal, and a closing sentence.
check: A response that explains why the opposing view is weaker
The first sentence of an essay
A list of sources at the end
Which phrase fits a formal argument?
I feel like it’s kind of true

learn: Verbals are verb forms used as other parts of speech. A gerund ends in -ing and acts as a noun (Swimming is fun). A participle acts as an adjective (the broken vase). An infinitive is to plus a verb (I want to read).

Active voice means the subject does the action: The dog chased the ball. Passive voice means the subject receives it: The ball was chased by the dog. Active voice is usually clearer, but passive is useful when the doer is unknown.

Verb mood shows the speaker’s attitude: indicative states facts, imperative gives commands, interrogative asks, conditional uses would or could, and subjunctive expresses wishes or unreal situations: If I were taller…
Avoid inappropriate shifts in voice or mood within a sentence. Use commas, ellipses (…) and dashes (—) to show pauses or breaks; an ellipsis can also show words left out of a quotation.
units.try: Find three passive-voice sentences in a textbook or write your own, then rewrite each in active voice. Next, write one sentence using the subjunctive mood starting with “If I were…”.
check: In “Running every day keeps her healthy,” the word “running” is a
Which sentence is in active voice?
The mural was painted by the students

learn: Research starts with a focused question. Use several credible sources, such as encyclopedias, government or university sites and expert books, and check who wrote each source, when, and why.
Paraphrase in your own words and quote only when the wording matters. Always cite your sources; using someone else’s words or ideas without credit is plagiarism.
Narratives use a clear point of view, pacing, dialogue, description and reflection. Strong narratives show events through sensory detail and use transitions to signal shifts in time or place.
When presenting, make eye contact, speak at a steady pace and volume, and use visuals that support rather than repeat your words. Practice once aloud with a timer before presenting.
units.try: Pick a question you are curious about, such as “How do bees communicate?” Find two credible sources, write three facts in your own words with the source for each, and give a one-minute talk to someone at home.
check: Using someone else’s words without giving credit is
Which is usually a more credible source for a science fact?

rooms.about: This course bridges arithmetic and algebra: real numbers, exponents, scientific notation, linear equations and systems, functions, transformations, the Pythagorean theorem, volume and bivariate data.

learn: A rational number can be written as a fraction a/b of two integers with b not 0. Its decimal either ends (0.75) or repeats forever (0.333…). Integers like −4 are rational because −4 = −4/1.
An irrational number cannot be written as a fraction. Its decimal never ends and never repeats. Examples are √2 ≈ 1.414, √5 and π ≈ 3.14159.
To estimate a square root, find the perfect squares around it. √50 is between √49 = 7 and √64 = 8, and closer to 7, so √50 ≈ 7.1.
A repeating decimal can be changed to a fraction. If x = 0.444…, then 10x = 4.444…; subtracting gives 9x = 4, so x = 4/9.
units.try:
Estimate √30 and change 0.181818… to a fraction.
Step 1: 25 < 30 < 36, so 5 < √30 < 6. 30 is 5 away from 25 and 6 away from 36, so √30 ≈ 5.5 (it is about 5.48).
Step 2: Let x = 0.1818…. Two digits repeat, so multiply by 100: 100x = 18.1818….
Step 3: Subtract: 100x − x = 18, so 99x = 18 and x = 18/99 = 2/11.
check: Between which two whole numbers is √70?

learn: An exponent tells how many times to multiply a base by itself: 2⁴ = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16. Any nonzero number to the zero power is 1, so 7⁰ = 1.
Product rule: when multiplying powers with the same base, add exponents: 3² × 3⁵ = 3⁷. Quotient rule: when dividing, subtract: 5⁶ ÷ 5² = 5⁴.
Power of a power: multiply exponents: (2³)² = 2⁶ = 64. A negative exponent means a reciprocal: 4⁻² = 1/4² = 1/16.
Square roots undo squaring and cube roots undo cubing. If x² = 49, then x = 7 or x = −7. If x³ = 27, then x = 3, because 3 × 3 × 3 = 27.
units.try:
Simplify (2³ × 2⁻⁵) ÷ 2⁻⁴.
Step 1: Product rule on top: 2³ × 2⁻⁵ = 2^(3 + (−5)) = 2⁻².
Step 2: Quotient rule: 2⁻² ÷ 2⁻⁴ = 2^(−2 − (−4)) = 2².
Step 3: 2² = 4. Answer: 4.

learn: Scientific notation writes a number as a × 10ⁿ, where 1 ≤ a < 10 and n is an integer. It makes very big or very small numbers easy to read.
For large numbers, move the decimal left and count the moves: 4,500,000 = 4.5 × 10⁶. For small numbers, move right and use a negative exponent: 0.00032 = 3.2 × 10⁻⁴.
To multiply, multiply the a parts and add exponents: (2 × 10³)(4 × 10⁵) = 8 × 10⁸. To divide, divide the a parts and subtract exponents.
If the result is not between 1 and 10, adjust: 15 × 10⁴ = 1.5 × 10⁵. Scientists use this form for distances like 1.5 × 10⁸ km from Earth to the Sun.
units.try:
Multiply (6 × 10⁴)(3 × 10⁻⁷).
Step 1: Multiply 6 × 3 = 18.
Step 2: Add exponents: 4 + (−7) = −3, giving 18 × 10⁻³.
Step 3: Adjust: 18 = 1.8 × 10¹, so the answer is 1.8 × 10⁻².

learn: A linear equation in one variable can be solved by doing the same operation to both sides to isolate the variable. Use the distributive property and combine like terms first.
Example: 3(x + 2) = 2x + 11. Distribute: 3x + 6 = 2x + 11. Subtract 2x: x + 6 = 11. Subtract 6: x = 5. Check: 3(7) = 21 and 2(5) + 11 = 21.

Some equations have one solution, some have no solution, and some have infinitely many. If you get a false statement like 4 = 7, there is no solution. If you get a true one like 4 = 4, every number works.
With variables on both sides, move all variable terms to one side first. With fractions, multiply both sides by the common denominator to clear them.
units.try:
Solve 5x − 4 = 2(x + 7).
Step 1: Distribute: 5x − 4 = 2x + 14.
Step 2: Subtract 2x from both sides: 3x − 4 = 14.
Step 3: Add 4: 3x = 18.
Step 4: Divide by 3: x = 6. Check: 5(6) − 4 = 26 and 2(13) = 26.

learn: Slope measures steepness: slope m = rise ÷ run = (y₂ − y₁) ÷ (x₂ − x₁). Between (1, 2) and (3, 8), m = (8 − 2) ÷ (3 − 1) = 3.
A positive slope rises left to right, a negative slope falls, a horizontal line has slope 0, and a vertical line has undefined slope.
A proportional relationship has the form y = kx and passes through (0, 0). The unit rate k is the slope. If 4 pounds cost $10, k = 2.5 dollars per pound.
Similar right triangles drawn on any line have the same rise-to-run ratio, which is why a line has one constant slope everywhere.
units.try:
Find the slope through (−2, 5) and (4, −1).
Step 1: Rise = −1 − 5 = −6.
Step 2: Run = 4 − (−2) = 6.
Step 3: m = −6 ÷ 6 = −1. The line falls one unit for each unit to the right.
check: What is the slope through (0, 1) and (2, 7)?

learn: Slope-intercept form is y = mx + b, where m is the slope and b is the y-intercept, the point where the line crosses the y-axis at (0, b).
To graph y = 2x − 3, plot (0, −3), then go up 2 and right 1 to (1, −1). Draw the line through the points.
To write an equation from two points, find m first, then substitute one point to solve for b. For (1, 5) and (3, 9): m = 2, then 5 = 2(1) + b, so b = 3 and y = 2x + 3.
In real situations, b is often a starting amount and m a rate. A taxi charging $3 plus $2 per mile is y = 2x + 3.
units.try:
A gym charges a $20 sign-up fee plus $15 per month. Write and use the equation.
Step 1: Rate m = 15, start b = 20, so y = 15x + 20.
Step 2: For 6 months: y = 15(6) + 20 = 90 + 20 = 110.
Step 3: The cost for 6 months is $110.
check: In y = −3x + 7, what is the y-intercept?
Which line has slope 4 and crosses the y-axis at −2?

learn: A system of equations is two or more equations with the same variables. The solution is the point that makes both true, where the lines intersect.
Two lines can cross once (one solution), be parallel with the same slope and different intercepts (no solution), or be the same line (infinitely many solutions).
Substitution: solve one equation for a variable and plug it into the other. Elimination: add or subtract equations to cancel a variable.
Example: y = 2x and x + y = 9. Substitute: x + 2x = 9, so 3x = 9, x = 3 and y = 6. The solution is (3, 6).
units.try:
Solve by elimination: x + y = 10 and x − y = 4.
Step 1: Add the equations: 2x = 14.
Step 2: x = 7.
Step 3: Substitute: 7 + y = 10, so y = 3.
Step 4: Check: 7 − 3 = 4. The solution is (7, 3).
check: Two lines with the same slope and different y-intercepts have

learn: A function is a rule that gives exactly one output for each input. In a table or set of points, no input (x) may repeat with different outputs.
The vertical line test: if any vertical line touches a graph more than once, the graph is not a function.
A linear function has a constant rate of change and a straight-line graph, such as f(x) = 3x + 1. A nonlinear function, such as f(x) = x², does not change at a constant rate.
Function notation f(x) is read “f of x.” If f(x) = 2x + 5, then f(4) = 2(4) + 5 = 13. Graphs can be described as increasing, decreasing or constant over intervals.
units.try:
Decide if the table x: 1, 2, 3, 4 and y: 5, 8, 11, 14 is a linear function.
Step 1: Each x appears once, so it is a function.
Step 2: The y values change by +3 each time x increases by 1, a constant rate.
Step 3: It is linear: start at x = 0 by subtracting 3 from 5 to get 2. So y = 3x + 2.
check: If f(x) = x² − 1, what is f(3)?
Which set of points is NOT a function?

units.t: Transformations, Angles and the Pythagorean Theorem
learn: Rigid transformations keep size and shape: translations slide, reflections flip, and rotations turn. Figures related by these are congruent. A dilation by scale factor k changes size, making similar figures.
Rules: translating (x, y) 3 right gives (x + 3, y); reflecting over the x-axis gives (x, −y); rotating 90° counterclockwise about the origin gives (−y, x); dilating by 2 gives (2x, 2y).
A triangle’s angles add to 180°. When a transversal crosses parallel lines, alternate interior angles are equal and same-side interior angles add to 180°.
The Pythagorean theorem: in a right triangle with legs a and b and hypotenuse c, a² + b² = c². It also finds distance between points on a grid.
units.try:
Find the distance between (1, 2) and (7, 10).
Step 1: Horizontal leg a = 7 − 1 = 6. Vertical leg b = 10 − 2 = 8.
Step 2: c² = 6² + 8² = 36 + 64 = 100.
Step 3: c = √100 = 10. The distance is 10 units.
check: A right triangle has legs 5 and 12. How long is the hypotenuse?

learn: Volume formulas: cylinder V = πr²h, cone V = (1/3)πr²h, sphere V = (4/3)πr³. A cone holds one third of a cylinder with the same base and height.

A scatter plot shows pairs of data as points. Patterns can show positive association (both rise), negative association (one rises as the other falls) or no association. Outliers are points far from the rest.
A line of best fit is a straight line drawn close to most points. Its slope shows the rate, and you can use it to make predictions.
A two-way table shows counts for two categories, such as grade level and whether students have a curfew. Relative frequencies (row or column percents) help compare groups.
units.try:
Find the volume of a cylinder with radius 3 cm and height 10 cm. Use π ≈ 3.14.
Step 1: r² = 3² = 9.
Step 2: V = π × 9 × 10 = 90π.
Step 3: 90 × 3.14 = 282.6. The volume is about 282.6 cm³.
check: What is the volume formula for a sphere?
Hours studied and test scores both rising together shows

rooms.about: Physical science explores matter and energy: atoms, the periodic table, chemical reactions, forces and motion, energy, waves, electricity and magnetism. You will plan investigations, measure carefully and explain results with evidence.

learn: Scientists ask testable questions and run fair tests. The independent variable is what you change, the dependent variable is what you measure, and controlled variables stay the same.

Scientists use the metric system (SI). Length is measured in meters, mass in grams or kilograms, volume in liters, temperature in degrees Celsius and time in seconds. Prefixes like kilo- (1,000) and milli- (1/1,000) scale units.
Precision is how close repeated measurements are to each other; accuracy is how close they are to the true value. Repeating trials and averaging results makes data more reliable.
Lab safety comes first: wear goggles, tie back hair, never taste chemicals, and report spills or broken glass to an adult right away.
units.try: Test how the height of a ramp affects how far a toy car rolls. Change only the ramp height (use 1, 2 and 3 books), keep the same car and floor, run three trials each, and average the distances. Name your independent, dependent and controlled variables.
check: In a fair test, the variable you deliberately change is the
How many milliliters are in 1 liter?

learn: Matter is anything with mass that takes up space. Physical properties, like color, density, melting point and boiling point, can be observed without changing what the substance is.
Density = mass ÷ volume. Water’s density is about 1 g/cm³. Objects denser than water sink; less dense objects float. A 20 g block with volume 10 cm³ has density 2 g/cm³ and sinks.
In solids, particles vibrate in fixed places; in liquids they slide past each other; in gases they move fast and spread out. Adding thermal energy speeds particles up and can cause a phase change.
Water melts at 0 °C and boils at 100 °C at sea level. During a phase change, temperature stays constant while energy breaks or forms attractions between particles.
units.try: Fill a clear cup with water. Predict, then test, whether a grape, a coin, a cork and an ice cube float or sink. Explain each result using density compared with water’s 1 g/cm³.
check: What is the density of an object with mass 30 g and volume 15 cm³?
In which state do particles move fastest and spread out the most?

learn: Atoms are made of protons (positive) and neutrons (no charge) in the nucleus, with electrons (negative) moving around it. The number of protons is the atomic number and defines the element.
Atoms with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons are isotopes. Carbon-12 and carbon-14 both have 6 protons but 6 and 8 neutrons.

The periodic table arranges elements by atomic number. Rows are periods; columns are groups, and elements in a group have similar properties because they have the same number of outer (valence) electrons.
Metals are on the left and middle, are shiny and conduct heat and electricity. Nonmetals are on the right. Metalloids, like silicon, lie along the zigzag line and have mixed properties.
units.try: Look at a periodic table. Find sodium (Na), chlorine (Cl) and neon (Ne). For each, write the atomic number, whether it is a metal or nonmetal, and its group. Notice that neon is in the last group, the noble gases, which rarely react.
check: What determines which element an atom is?
The number of electron shells only
Elements in the same column of the periodic table

learn: In a chemical change, atoms rearrange to form new substances. Signs include a color change, gas bubbles, a new solid (precipitate), light, or a temperature change.

A chemical equation shows reactants turning into products: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. Atoms are not created or destroyed, so the equation must be balanced with the same number of each atom on both sides. This is the law of conservation of mass.
Exothermic reactions release energy, often as heat; burning is an example. Endothermic reactions absorb energy, like an instant cold pack.
Reaction rates increase with higher temperature, higher concentration, more surface area (smaller pieces) and catalysts, which speed reactions without being used up.
units.try: With an adult, mix one spoon of baking soda with a quarter cup of vinegar in a cup. Observe the bubbles (carbon dioxide gas). Touch the outside of the cup: is it cooler? Write which signs of a chemical reaction you saw.
check: Which is a sign of a chemical change?
A new gas forms as bubbles
A reaction that releases heat is

learn: A force is a push or pull measured in newtons (N). Net force is the total of all forces. Balanced forces (net force 0) do not change motion; unbalanced forces cause acceleration.
Newton’s first law: an object keeps doing what it is doing unless an unbalanced force acts on it. This tendency is inertia, and more mass means more inertia.
Newton’s second law: F = m × a. A 2 kg cart pushed with 10 N accelerates at 10 ÷ 2 = 5 m/s². Newton’s third law: for every action there is an equal and opposite reaction.
Friction opposes motion between surfaces. Gravity attracts all masses; on Earth it pulls with about 9.8 N on each kilogram, which is an object’s weight.
units.try:
Use F = m × a. A 50 kg skater accelerates at 2 m/s². What force is needed?
Step 1: Write the formula: F = m × a.
Step 2: Substitute: F = 50 × 2.
Step 3: F = 100 N.
check: What is the acceleration of a 4 kg object pushed with a net force of 20 N?
A rocket pushes gas down and the gas pushes the rocket up. This shows
The law of conservation of mass

learn: Speed = distance ÷ time. A runner covering 100 m in 20 s has an average speed of 5 m/s.
Velocity is speed with a direction, such as 5 m/s north. Acceleration is the change in velocity ÷ time; speeding up, slowing down and turning are all accelerations.
On a distance-time graph, a steeper line means faster motion and a flat line means the object is stopped. On a speed-time graph, a rising line shows acceleration.
Momentum = mass × velocity. In a collision, total momentum is conserved, which is why a heavy truck is harder to stop than a bicycle at the same speed.
units.try: Time yourself walking 20 meters (measure with steps of about 1 meter or a tape). Calculate your speed with speed = distance ÷ time. Then walk it faster and compare. Sketch a distance-time graph for both walks.
check: A car travels 150 km in 3 hours. What is its average speed?
What does a flat line on a distance-time graph mean?
The object is moving backward fast

learn: Energy is the ability to do work or cause change, measured in joules (J). Kinetic energy is energy of motion: KE = ½mv². Doubling speed makes kinetic energy four times as large.
Potential energy is stored energy. Gravitational potential energy = mgh (mass × 9.8 × height). A ball held higher has more stored energy.
Energy changes forms but is never created or destroyed. On a roller coaster, potential energy at the top changes to kinetic energy at the bottom, while some becomes heat from friction.
Thermal energy moves from hot to cold by conduction (touch), convection (flowing liquids or gases) and radiation (waves, like sunlight).
units.try:
Find the kinetic energy of a 2 kg ball moving at 3 m/s.
Step 1: KE = ½mv².
Step 2: v² = 3² = 9.
Step 3: KE = ½ × 2 × 9 = 9 J.
check: If an object’s speed doubles, its kinetic energy becomes
Heat moving through a metal spoon in hot soup is

learn: A wave carries energy without carrying matter along. Wavelength is the distance between crests, frequency is waves per second (hertz, Hz), and amplitude is the wave’s height, related to energy.
Wave speed = frequency × wavelength. Sound is a mechanical wave that needs a medium; it travels about 343 m/s in air and faster in water and solids. Higher frequency sounds have higher pitch.

Light is an electromagnetic wave and can travel through empty space at about 300,000 km/s. The spectrum runs from radio waves through microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays.
Waves can be reflected (bounce), refracted (bend when changing medium), absorbed or transmitted. Digital signals send information as pulses, which are more reliable than analog signals.
units.try:
Find the speed of a wave with frequency 5 Hz and wavelength 2 m.
Step 1: speed = frequency × wavelength.
Step 2: speed = 5 × 2 = 10 m/s.
Then put a pencil in a glass of water and observe how refraction makes it look bent.
check: Which kind of wave can travel through empty space?
Higher frequency sound is heard as

learn: Electric current is the flow of charge, measured in amperes. Voltage is the push, measured in volts, and resistance slows current, measured in ohms. Ohm’s law: V = I × R.
A series circuit has one path, so if one bulb goes out, all go out. A parallel circuit has several paths, so other bulbs stay lit; homes are wired in parallel.
Magnets have north and south poles; like poles repel and opposite poles attract. A magnetic field surrounds a magnet. Earth itself acts like a giant magnet.
Electricity and magnetism are linked. A current in a coiled wire makes an electromagnet, and moving a magnet through a coil generates current, which is how generators work.
units.try:
Use Ohm’s law. A 9 V battery is connected to a 3 Ω resistor. What is the current?
Step 1: V = I × R, so I = V ÷ R.
Step 2: I = 9 ÷ 3 = 3 A.
Safety: never experiment with wall outlets.
check: In which circuit do the other bulbs stay lit if one burns out?
Two north poles of magnets placed together will

learn: Gravity is an attractive force between any two masses. It grows stronger with more mass and weaker with more distance. The Moon’s gravity is about 1/6 of Earth’s.
Gravitational, electric and magnetic forces act at a distance through fields; objects do not need to touch.
Energy resources are renewable (solar, wind, hydroelectric, geothermal) or nonrenewable (coal, oil, natural gas, uranium). Each has benefits and costs for price, reliability and the environment.
Engineers design solutions by defining criteria and constraints, testing models and improving them. A design that keeps a drink cold longest might compare different insulating materials.
units.try: Design a simple insulator: wrap three identical cups of ice water in different materials (cloth, foil, paper) and leave one unwrapped. Check after 30 minutes which kept the most ice. Explain using how thermal energy moves.
check: How does distance affect gravity between two objects?
Which is a renewable energy resource?

rooms.about: This course traces American history from the first peoples and European colonies through the Revolution, the Constitution, westward expansion, slavery and the Civil War, to the end of Reconstruction in 1877.

learn: People lived in the Americas for at least 15,000 years before Europeans arrived. Hundreds of Native nations, such as the Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) Confederacy, the Pueblo peoples and the Cherokee, built farms, trade networks and governments.

In 1492 Christopher Columbus, sailing for Spain, reached the Caribbean. Spain, Portugal, France, the Netherlands and England then explored and claimed lands, seeking gold, trade routes and converts to Christianity.

The Columbian Exchange moved plants, animals and people between hemispheres. Corn and potatoes went to Europe; horses and wheat came to the Americas. European diseases such as smallpox killed a very large share of Native people.
Spanish conquest brought forced labor systems, and the Atlantic slave trade began carrying enslaved Africans to the Americas in brutal conditions.
units.try: Make a two-column chart titled Columbian Exchange. List at least four items that went from the Americas to Europe, Africa and Asia, and four that came to the Americas. Circle one item that changed daily life the most and explain why in two sentences.
check: The transfer of plants, animals, people and diseases between hemispheres
A treaty between Spain and England
Which caused the greatest loss of Native lives after 1492?

learn: England founded Jamestown, Virginia, in 1607, its first lasting colony. Tobacco became its cash crop. In 1619 the first recorded enslaved Africans arrived there, and the House of Burgesses became the first elected assembly.

The New England colonies, such as Massachusetts, were founded largely by Puritans seeking to build religious communities. Their economy relied on fishing, shipbuilding and small farms, and town meetings practiced local self-government.

The Middle colonies, like Pennsylvania and New York, were diverse and grew wheat, earning the name breadbasket colonies. The Southern colonies grew tobacco, rice and indigo on plantations dependent on enslaved labor.
The Mayflower Compact of 1620 was an agreement to make fair laws for the common good, an early example of self-government.
units.try: Draw a simple map of the eastern coast and divide it into New England, Middle and Southern colonies. For each region, write its climate, main ways of earning a living and one important fact about who lived there.
check: What was England’s first permanent colony in North America?
The Middle colonies were called the breadbasket colonies because they grew lots of

learn: After the French and Indian War ended in 1763, Britain had large debts and taxed the colonies with laws such as the Stamp Act (1765) and the Townshend Acts. Colonists protested “no taxation without representation.”

Tensions grew. In the Boston Massacre of 1770, British soldiers killed five colonists. In the Boston Tea Party of 1773, protesters dumped British tea into the harbor. Britain answered with the Intolerable Acts.
In April 1775 fighting began at Lexington and Concord. The Second Continental Congress formed the Continental Army under George Washington.

On July 4, 1776, Congress adopted the Declaration of Independence, written mainly by Thomas Jefferson. It stated that all men are created equal with rights to life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness, though slavery and unequal rights continued.
units.try: Create a timeline from 1763 to 1776 with at least six events. For each, write one sentence explaining how it increased tension between the colonists and Britain.
check: What did “no taxation without representation” mean?
Colonists objected to taxes passed without their own elected representatives
Colonists wanted no taxes of any kind ever
Who was the main author of the Declaration of Independence?

learn: The Continental Army faced the world’s strongest military. Washington kept the army together through hard winters such as Valley Forge in 1777 to 1778.
The American victory at Saratoga in 1777 convinced France to join as an ally, sending troops, money and a navy. Spain and the Netherlands also aided the Americans.

Women supported the war by running farms and businesses, and some served in camps or even in battle. About 5,000 Black soldiers fought for the Patriots, while thousands of enslaved people joined the British, who promised freedom. Many Native nations sided with Britain to protect their lands.
The British surrendered at Yorktown in 1781. The Treaty of Paris (1783) recognized American independence and set the western border at the Mississippi River.
units.try: Write a short diary entry as a soldier at Valley Forge in winter. Include at least three historically accurate details about conditions, such as cold, hunger or training under Baron von Steuben.
check: Which battle convinced France to ally with the Americans?
Which treaty ended the Revolutionary War?

learn: The first national government, under the Articles of Confederation, was weak: it could not tax, had no national courts, and needed 9 of 13 states to pass laws. Shays’ Rebellion in 1786 showed its problems.
In 1787 delegates met in Philadelphia. The Great Compromise created a two-house Congress: the Senate with two members per state and the House of Representatives based on population.
The Three-Fifths Compromise counted three of every five enslaved people for representation, increasing Southern power in Congress. The delegates also agreed not to ban the slave trade until 1808.
Federalists supported the Constitution; Anti-Federalists feared a strong central government. The promise of a Bill of Rights, the first ten amendments, adopted in 1791, helped win ratification.
units.try: Make a chart comparing the Articles of Confederation and the Constitution on four features: power to tax, executive leader, national courts and how laws are passed. Write one sentence on which weakness you think mattered most and why.
check: A Congress with a Senate and a House of Representatives
What are the first ten amendments to the Constitution called?

learn: The Constitution rests on popular sovereignty (power comes from the people), limited government, and federalism, the sharing of power between national and state governments.
Separation of powers divides government into three branches: legislative (Congress makes laws), executive (the President carries out laws) and judicial (courts interpret laws).

Checks and balances let each branch limit the others. The President can veto a bill; Congress can override with a two-thirds vote; courts can rule laws unconstitutional, a power called judicial review from Marbury v. Madison (1803).
The Bill of Rights protects freedoms such as speech, religion, press and assembly (First Amendment), and rights of people accused of crimes, like a fair and speedy trial.
units.try: Draw three connected circles labeled legislative, executive and judicial. On the arrows between them, write one check each branch has on another. Then list three freedoms in the First Amendment.
check: What vote does Congress need to override a presidential veto?

learn: George Washington became the first President in 1789. His Treasury Secretary, Alexander Hamilton, created a national bank; Thomas Jefferson opposed it, and the first political parties formed from their disagreements.
In his Farewell Address, Washington warned against political parties and permanent foreign alliances. In 1800 power passed peacefully from one party to another when Jefferson was elected.
In 1803 Jefferson bought the Louisiana Territory from France for about $15 million, doubling the nation’s size. Lewis and Clark explored it with the help of Sacagawea, a Shoshone woman.
The War of 1812 against Britain was fought over trade and sailors’ rights. The Monroe Doctrine (1823) warned European powers not to create new colonies in the Americas.
units.try: On an outline map of the United States, shade the original states and the Louisiana Purchase in different colors. Trace the route of Lewis and Clark from St. Louis to the Pacific and label three landmarks.
check: Which purchase doubled the size of the United States in 1803?
What did the Monroe Doctrine warn against?
New European colonies in the Americas

learn: Andrew Jackson, elected in 1828, expanded voting for white men. Under the Indian Removal Act (1830), the government forced Native nations west. On the Trail of Tears, about 4,000 of 16,000 Cherokee died.

Manifest destiny was the belief that the United States should spread across the continent. Texas became independent from Mexico in 1836 and joined the U.S. in 1845. After the Mexican-American War (1846 to 1848), Mexico lost about half its territory.
The Industrial Revolution brought factories, canals and railroads, especially in the North. The cotton gin (1793) made cotton very profitable and greatly expanded slavery in the South.

Reformers worked to end slavery (abolition), improve schools and prisons, and win rights for women. The Seneca Falls Convention of 1848, led by Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Lucretia Mott, called for women’s right to vote.
units.try: Write a short paragraph explaining how one invention, the cotton gin, changed both the economy and the lives of enslaved people. Use at least two specific facts.
check: What was the Trail of Tears?
The forced removal of the Cherokee and other nations westward
The Seneca Falls Convention of 1848 focused on

units.t: Slavery, Sectionalism and the Civil War
learn: Slavery was the central cause of growing division. By 1860 about 4 million people were enslaved. Enslaved people resisted in many ways, and some escaped on the Underground Railroad, helped by Harriet Tubman and others.

Compromises failed: the Missouri Compromise (1820), the Compromise of 1850 with its harsh Fugitive Slave Act, and the Kansas-Nebraska Act (1854). The Dred Scott decision (1857) said Black Americans were not citizens.

After Abraham Lincoln’s election in 1860, eleven Southern states seceded and formed the Confederacy. The war began at Fort Sumter in April 1861 and lasted until 1865, killing about 620,000 to 750,000 soldiers.

The Emancipation Proclamation (1863) freed enslaved people in Confederate areas, and about 180,000 Black soldiers joined the Union army. The Union victory at Gettysburg in 1863 was a turning point. Lee surrendered at Appomattox in April 1865.
units.try: Make a cause-and-effect chain of five boxes from the Missouri Compromise to the attack on Fort Sumter. In each box, write the event, the year and how it increased conflict over slavery.
check: What did the Emancipation Proclamation do?
Declared enslaved people in Confederate areas free
Gave women the right to vote
Where did the Civil War begin in 1861?

learn: Reconstruction (1865 to 1877) was the effort to rebuild the South and define freedom. Lincoln was assassinated in April 1865, and conflicts followed between Congress and President Andrew Johnson.
Three amendments changed the nation: the 13th abolished slavery (1865), the 14th granted citizenship and equal protection (1868), and the 15th barred denying the vote based on race (1870).
The Freedmen’s Bureau built schools and helped formerly enslaved people. Black Americans voted and held office; Hiram Revels became the first Black U.S. senator in 1870.

Many white Southerners resisted with Black Codes, violence by groups like the Ku Klux Klan, and sharecropping that trapped families in debt. After the Compromise of 1877, federal troops left the South and many gains were rolled back.
units.try: Make a chart of the 13th, 14th and 15th Amendments with the year, what each did, and one way its promise was later limited or ignored. Write a sentence about why these amendments still matter today.
check: The withdrawal of federal troops from the South

rooms.about: Spanish I builds a solid foundation: pronunciation, greetings, nouns and articles, adjective agreement, present-tense verbs, ser and estar, gustar, ir a plus infinitive and stem-changing verbs, with culture from Spanish-speaking countries throughout.

learn: Spanish vowels are short and always the same: a (ah), e (eh), i (ee), o (oh), u (oo). The letter h is silent (hola), ñ sounds like ny (año), ll sounds like y (llamar), and j sounds like a strong h (jugar).
Greetings: Hola (hello), Buenos días (good morning), Buenas tardes (good afternoon), Buenas noches (good evening or night). To ask how someone is: ¿Cómo estás? (friend) or ¿Cómo está usted? (formal).
Introduce yourself: Me llamo Ana (my name is Ana). ¿Cómo te llamas? (What is your name?). Mucho gusto (nice to meet you). Adiós (goodbye), Hasta luego (see you later).
Spanish writes questions and exclamations with marks at both ends: ¿Qué tal? and ¡Qué bien! In many Spanish-speaking countries, friends greet with a light kiss on the cheek or a handshake.
units.try:
Practice a dialogue aloud with a family member:
A: ¡Hola! Me llamo Sam. ¿Cómo te llamas?
B: Me llamo Luz. Mucho gusto.
A: Igualmente. ¿Cómo estás?
B: Muy bien, gracias. ¿Y tú?
A: Bien. ¡Hasta luego!
check: How do you say “What is your name?” to a friend?
Which letter is silent in Spanish?

learn: Numbers 0 to 15: cero, uno, dos, tres, cuatro, cinco, seis, siete, ocho, nueve, diez, once, doce, trece, catorce, quince. Then dieciséis, diecisiete, dieciocho, diecinueve, veinte (20), treinta (30), cuarenta (40), cincuenta (50), cien (100).
Days (lowercase in Spanish): lunes, martes, miércoles, jueves, viernes, sábado, domingo. Months: enero, febrero, marzo, abril, mayo, junio, julio, agosto, septiembre, octubre, noviembre, diciembre.
Dates put the day first: Hoy es el 5 de mayo (Today is May 5). The first of a month is el primero. ¿Cuándo es tu cumpleaños? means When is your birthday?
Telling time: ¿Qué hora es? Es la una (1:00). Son las tres (3:00). Son las cuatro y media (4:30). Son las seis y cuarto (6:15). Son las ocho menos diez (7:50).
units.try: Say your birthday in Spanish (Mi cumpleaños es el … de …). Then look at a clock five times today and say the time in Spanish each time, such as Son las dos y veinte.
check: How do you say 4:30 in Spanish?

learn: Every Spanish noun has a gender. Most nouns ending in -o are masculine (el libro, book) and most ending in -a are feminine (la mesa, table). Some exceptions: el día, el mapa, la mano.
Definite articles mean the: el (masc. singular), la (fem. singular), los (masc. plural), las (fem. plural). Indefinite articles mean a, an or some: un, una, unos, unas.
To make plurals, add -s to words ending in a vowel (libro → libros) and -es to words ending in a consonant (papel → papeles; lápiz → lápices, as z changes to c).
Classroom words: el cuaderno (notebook), el lápiz (pencil), la mochila (backpack), la computadora (computer), el escritorio (desk), la profesora (teacher). Useful phrase: ¿Cómo se dice … en español?
units.try: Label ten objects in your room with sticky notes in Spanish, including the article, such as la ventana (window), la puerta (door), el reloj (clock). Say each one aloud, then make three of them plural.
check: What is the plural of el lápiz?

learn: Ser means to be and is used for identity, origin, descriptions and professions. Forms: yo soy, tú eres, él/ella/usted es, nosotros somos, vosotros sois, ellos/ellas/ustedes son.
Adjectives agree with nouns in gender and number and usually come after the noun: el chico alto, la chica alta, los chicos altos, las chicas altas.
Adjectives ending in -e or a consonant have one form for both genders: inteligente, fácil, joven. Just add -s or -es for plural: inteligentes, jóvenes.
Common adjectives: alto (tall), bajo (short), simpático (nice), divertido (fun), serio (serious), trabajador (hardworking), perezoso (lazy). Origin: Soy de Texas. Ella es de México.
units.try: Write and say four sentences describing yourself and a friend using ser and adjectives that agree: Yo soy alto y simpático. Mi amiga Rosa es inteligente y divertida. Somos trabajadores. Somos de Ohio.

learn: Spanish verbs end in -ar, -er or -ir. To conjugate a regular -ar verb like hablar (to speak), drop -ar and add: -o, -as, -a, -amos, -áis, -an.
Hablar: yo hablo, tú hablas, él/ella habla, nosotros hablamos, vosotros habláis, ellos hablan. Subject pronouns are often dropped because the ending shows who: Hablo español.
Common -ar verbs: estudiar (study), trabajar (work), escuchar (listen), bailar (dance), cantar (sing), nadar (swim), tomar (take, drink), caminar (walk), necesitar (need).
To make a sentence negative, put no before the verb: No bailo bien. To ask a yes or no question, raise your voice at the end or invert: ¿Estudias tú mucho?
units.try: Conjugate cantar for all six forms aloud. Then write five sentences about what your family does on weekends, like Mi papá trabaja. Nosotros caminamos en el parque. Yo no nado.
check: What is the yo form of estudiar?
Choose the correct form: Ellos ___ música.

learn: Regular -er verbs like comer (to eat) take -o, -es, -e, -emos, -éis, -en: como, comes, come, comemos, coméis, comen.
Regular -ir verbs like vivir (to live) take -o, -es, -e, -imos, -ís, -en: vivo, vives, vive, vivimos, vivís, viven. Only the nosotros and vosotros forms differ from -er verbs.
Useful verbs: beber (drink), leer (read), aprender (learn), correr (run), escribir (write), abrir (open), compartir (share), recibir (receive).
School subjects: las matemáticas, las ciencias, el inglés, el arte, la historia, la educación física. Tengo la clase de ciencias en la segunda hora (I have science second period).
units.try: Write your class schedule in Spanish: En la primera hora, tengo matemáticas. Then write three sentences using -er and -ir verbs, such as Aprendo mucho en la clase de historia and Escribimos en el cuaderno.
check: What is the nosotros form of vivir?

learn: Gustar means to be pleasing. To say I like, use Me gusta + a singular noun or verb: Me gusta el fútbol. Me gusta leer. Use Me gustan + a plural noun: Me gustan los videojuegos.
Change the pronoun for the person: me (me), te (you), le (him, her, you formal), nos (us), os (you all), les (them). ¿Te gusta nadar? Sí, me gusta nadar. A ella le gustan los perros.
To say you do not like something: No me gusta correr. Use mucho for a lot and nada for not at all: No me gusta nada.

Free-time words: jugar al básquetbol, montar en bicicleta, ver la televisión, escuchar música, dibujar, ir al cine. Soccer, called fútbol, is the most popular sport in most Spanish-speaking countries.
units.try: Interview two people at home in Spanish: ¿Te gusta …? Ask about five activities. Then write a summary: A mi mamá le gusta leer, pero no le gusta correr.
check: How do you say “We like to dance”?

learn: Estar also means to be. Use it for location, feelings and temporary conditions. Forms: estoy, estás, está, estamos, estáis, están.
Feelings: Estoy cansado (tired), contento (happy), triste (sad), nervioso (nervous), enfermo (sick), aburrido (bored). Adjectives agree: Ella está cansada.
Location: ¿Dónde está la biblioteca? La biblioteca está al lado del gimnasio. Prepositions: cerca de (near), lejos de (far from), delante de (in front of), detrás de (behind), entre (between).
Remember the difference: ser for what something is (La sopa es deliciosa), estar for how or where it is now (La sopa está fría). The contraction de + el becomes del.
units.try: Describe your home: write where five rooms or things are, like La cocina está al lado de la sala. Then tell how you feel at three times today: Por la mañana estoy cansado.
check: Which verb do you use for location?

units.t: Ir, Ir a + Infinitive and Tener
learn: Ir (to go) is irregular: voy, vas, va, vamos, vais, van. Use a to show where: Voy a la escuela. A + el becomes al: Vamos al parque.
Ir a + infinitive talks about the near future: Voy a estudiar esta noche (I am going to study tonight). ¿Qué vas a hacer el sábado?
Tener (to have) is irregular: tengo, tienes, tiene, tenemos, tenéis, tienen. It appears in expressions: tener hambre (be hungry), tener sed (be thirsty), tener frío, tener calor, tener sueño.
Age uses tener: Tengo catorce años (I am 14 years old). Tener que + infinitive means have to: Tengo que hacer la tarea.
units.try: Write a plan for next weekend with five sentences using ir a + infinitive, such as El sábado voy a jugar al fútbol. Add two sentences with tener que, like Tengo que limpiar mi cuarto.
check: How do you say “I am 13 years old”?
Complete: Ellos ___ a comer pizza mañana.

learn: Some verbs change their stem in all forms except nosotros and vosotros. E→IE: querer (quiero, quieres, quiere, queremos, queréis, quieren). O→UE: poder (puedo, puedes, puede, podemos, podéis, pueden). E→I: pedir (pido, pides, pide, pedimos).
Jugar changes u→ue: juego, juegas, juega, jugamos. Other examples: pensar (pienso), dormir (duermo), volver (vuelvo), servir (sirvo).
Family words: el padre, la madre, el hermano, la hermana, los abuelos, el tío, la tía, el primo, la prima. Possessives: mi, tu, su, nuestro: Mi hermana tiene doce años.

Spanish is spoken by more than 480 million native speakers in over 20 countries. Traditions include the Day of the Dead (el Día de los Muertos) in Mexico on November 1 and 2, honoring loved ones who have died.
units.try: Draw your family tree and label each person in Spanish with a sentence: Mi abuela se llama Carmen. Then write three sentences using stem-changing verbs, like Mi hermano juega al béisbol and Yo quiero un perro.
check: What is the yo form of dormir?

rooms.about: Grade 8 Art deepens your use of the elements and principles of design through drawing, painting, printmaking, sculpture and digital art, while you study art across cultures, critique work and build a small portfolio.

units.t: Elements and Principles of Design Review
learn: The elements of art are the building blocks: line, shape, form, color, value, space and texture. Shape is flat (2D); form has depth (3D).
The principles of design are how artists arrange the elements: balance, contrast, emphasis, movement, pattern, rhythm, proportion, variety and unity.
Balance can be symmetrical (mirror-like on both sides), asymmetrical (different but equal in visual weight) or radial (spreading from a center, like a flower).
Emphasis creates a focal point, the place the eye goes first. Artists create it with contrast in color or value, size, isolation or lines that point toward it.
units.try: Make a small design using only black marker on paper. Use at least four kinds of line (straight, curved, zigzag, dotted) and create one clear focal point through contrast. Then write which principles you used.
check: Which is an element of art rather than a principle?
A design that spreads out from a center point shows

learn: Observational drawing means drawing what you actually see, not what you think something looks like. Look at the subject more than at your paper.
Contour drawing traces edges with one continuous line. Blind contour drawing is done without looking at the paper; it trains your eye and hand to work together.
Measure proportions with your pencil: hold it at arm’s length, close one eye, and compare lengths, such as a bottle being three times as tall as it is wide.
Gesture drawings are quick (30 to 60 seconds) and capture movement and pose rather than detail. Artists warm up with gestures before longer drawings.
units.try: Set a shoe on a table. Do a two-minute blind contour drawing, then a ten-minute careful contour drawing using pencil measuring for proportions. Compare the two and note what you noticed by looking closely.
check: Drawing the edges while not looking at the paper
Drawing with your eyes closed and no subject
Gesture drawings are mainly meant to capture

learn: Value is how light or dark a color is. A value scale shows steps from white to black. Strong contrast between light and dark makes drawings look dramatic and 3D.
Shading a sphere includes the highlight (brightest spot), midtones, core shadow, reflected light (a faint lightening near the edge) and the cast shadow on the ground.
Shading techniques: hatching (parallel lines), cross-hatching (crossing lines), stippling (dots) and blending (smooth tones with a tissue or stump).
Chiaroscuro is the use of strong light and dark contrast to model form, used by artists like Caravaggio and Rembrandt in the 1600s.
units.try: Draw a value scale with seven boxes from white to black using pencil. Then shine a flashlight on a ball in a dim room and draw it, including the highlight, core shadow, reflected light and cast shadow.
check: Shading with lines that cross each other
The shadow an object throws onto the surface beneath it is the

learn: Perspective creates the illusion of depth on a flat surface. Overlapping, size change (far things smaller), placement (far things higher) and atmospheric perspective (far things paler and bluer) all show distance.

Linear perspective uses a horizon line at eye level and vanishing points where parallel lines appear to meet. It was developed in Italy in the 1400s; Filippo Brunelleschi is credited with demonstrating it.
In one-point perspective, lines going away from you meet at one vanishing point, like railroad tracks. In two-point perspective, an object seen from a corner uses two vanishing points.
Lines that run straight up and down stay vertical in both one- and two-point perspective.
units.try: Draw a horizon line and one vanishing point. Draw a road that narrows to the point, then add three buildings with sides that angle toward it. Add windows and doors that also follow the lines.
check: Where do parallel lines appear to meet in linear perspective?
At the bottom of the page
At the focal point of color
In atmospheric perspective, distant mountains look

learn: Primary colors are red, yellow and blue. Secondary colors (orange, green, violet) mix two primaries. Tertiary colors mix a primary with a nearby secondary, like red-orange.
Complementary colors sit opposite on the color wheel (red and green, blue and orange). Side by side they create strong contrast; mixed they make neutral browns and grays.
A tint adds white, a shade adds black, and a tone adds gray. Warm colors (red, orange, yellow) seem to come forward; cool colors (blue, green, violet) seem to move back.
Color schemes include monochromatic (one hue in many values), analogous (neighbors on the wheel) and complementary. Watercolor uses water to thin paint; acrylic dries quickly and can be layered.
units.try: Paint a 12-part color wheel with only red, yellow, blue and white. Then paint a small landscape using only an analogous color scheme, such as blue, blue-green and green.
check: What is the complement of blue?
Adding white to a color makes a

learn: Printmaking makes multiple copies of an image from a carved or prepared surface. Each copy is a print, and a numbered group is an edition, written like 3/10.
In relief printing, you carve away areas you do not want to print; the raised surface takes the ink. Woodcuts and linocuts are relief prints.
Remember that prints come out reversed, so letters must be carved backward.
Japanese ukiyo-e woodblock prints from the 1600s to 1800s, like Hokusai’s The Great Wave, influenced European artists. Safe beginner printing uses foam sheets pressed with a pencil.
units.try: Draw a simple design on a clean foam tray, pressing lines in with a dull pencil. Roll or brush washable paint over it, press paper on top, and rub with your palm. Peel it off and make two more prints.
check: In relief printing, which part takes the ink?
The raised surface left after carving
What does the number 3/10 on a print mean?
It is the third print in an edition of ten
It took three of ten days

learn: Sculpture is three-dimensional art viewed from all sides. Additive sculpture builds up material, like clay modeling. Subtractive sculpture removes material, like carving stone or soap.
Relief sculpture projects from a flat background, like faces on a coin. Freestanding sculpture, or sculpture in the round, can be walked around.
Clay hand-building methods include pinch pots, coil building and slab construction. To join clay, score (scratch) both surfaces and add slip, a watery clay glue.
Armatures are inner skeletons, often wire, that support sculptures. Artists consider positive space (the form) and negative space (the empty areas around and through it).
units.try: With an adult’s help, carve a simple animal from a bar of soap using a plastic knife or spoon (subtractive), or build a small coil pot from air-dry clay (additive). Turn it as you work so it looks good from every side.
check: Carving soap is an example of
What is slip used for in clay work?

learn: Art reflects the beliefs and lives of the people who made it. Cave paintings at Lascaux, France, are about 17,000 years old. Ancient Egyptian art followed strict rules showing figures with heads in profile.
West African masks, like those of the Dan and Yoruba peoples, are used in ceremonies with music and dance. Islamic art often uses geometric patterns and calligraphy.

The Renaissance (about 1400 to 1600) brought realism and perspective; Leonardo da Vinci and Michelangelo are famous examples. Impressionists in the 1870s, like Claude Monet, painted outdoor light with quick brushstrokes.
Twentieth-century movements include Cubism (Pablo Picasso), the Harlem Renaissance (Jacob Lawrence, Augusta Savage) and Mexican muralism (Diego Rivera, who painted large public murals).
units.try: Choose one artwork from a culture different from your own (look in a library book). Sketch it, then write who made it or which culture, about when, what materials were used, and what purpose it might have served.
check: Which movement focused on capturing light with quick brushstrokes?
Diego Rivera is best known for

learn: Graphic design communicates ideas with images and text, like posters, logos and book covers. Good design is clear, readable and uses contrast, alignment, repetition and proximity.
Typography is the art of arranging letters. Serif fonts have small feet on letters; sans serif fonts do not. Use no more than two or three fonts in one design.
Digital images are made of pixels. Raster images lose quality when enlarged; vector images use math-based lines and stay sharp at any size, so logos are usually vectors.
Respect copyright: use your own photos and drawings or images that are clearly free to use, and give credit to creators.
units.try: Design a poster for an imaginary school event, by hand or on a computer. Include a clear title, date and place, one strong image, and no more than two fonts. Check that someone can read it from across a room.
check: Why are logos usually made as vector images?
They stay sharp at any size
A font with small feet on the ends of letters is a

learn: An art critique follows four steps: describe (what you see), analyze (how elements and principles are used), interpret (what it means or expresses), and judge (how well it succeeds and why).
Give feedback that is specific and kind: name one strength, one question and one suggestion. “The cast shadow makes the vase look solid; maybe darken the background for more contrast.”
A portfolio is a collection of your best work that shows growth and range. Include finished pieces and a few sketches that show your process.
An artist statement is a short paragraph explaining your ideas, materials and choices, written in first person.
units.try: Pick three artworks you made this year. For each, write a two-sentence artist statement. Then critique one using the four steps: describe, analyze, interpret and judge.
check: What is the first step of an art critique?
What does a good portfolio show?
Your best work, growth and range
Every scrap of paper you used
Only work copied from famous artists

rooms.about: Grade 8 Music builds reading and listening skills: rhythm, meter, notes, scales, chords, form and expression, plus a tour of music history, world music and American styles, and composing and performing your own music.

learn: Rhythm is the pattern of long and short sounds. Note values: a whole note gets 4 beats in 4/4 time, a half note 2, a quarter note 1, an eighth note ½ and a sixteenth note ¼. Rests are silences of the same lengths.
A time signature has two numbers. The top tells how many beats are in each measure; the bottom tells which note gets the beat. In 3/4, there are 3 quarter-note beats per measure, as in a waltz.
A dot adds half the note’s value: a dotted half note equals 3 beats. A tie connects two notes of the same pitch into one longer sound.
Tempo is the speed, measured in beats per minute (BPM). Italian terms: largo (very slow), andante (walking pace), allegro (fast), presto (very fast).
units.try: Clap and count this 4/4 rhythm aloud: quarter, quarter, half | eighth eighth, quarter, quarter, quarter | dotted half, quarter. Count “1, 2, 3-4 | 1 and, 2, 3, 4 | 1-2-3, 4.” Then clap it at a slow tempo and a fast tempo.
check: How many beats does a dotted half note get in 4/4 time?

learn: The staff has five lines and four spaces. The treble clef is used for higher sounds; its line notes are E, G, B, D, F and its space notes spell F, A, C, E.
The bass clef is used for lower sounds; its line notes are G, B, D, F, A and its space notes are A, C, E, G. Middle C sits on a short ledger line between the two clefs.
A sharp (♯) raises a note one half step, a flat (♭) lowers it a half step, and a natural (♮) cancels them. On a piano, a half step is the very next key, black or white.
The musical alphabet uses only seven letters, A through G, then repeats. The distance from one C to the next C is an octave.
units.try: Draw a treble staff and write these notes: E, F, G, A, B, C, D, E, F. Label each. Make up a sentence to remember the line notes E G B D F, such as Every Good Bird Does Fly.
check: What are the space notes of the treble clef?
What does a flat do to a note?

learn: A major scale follows the pattern whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half. C major uses only white keys: C D E F G A B C.
A natural minor scale follows whole, half, whole, whole, half, whole, whole. A minor uses the same notes as C major but starts on A, so they are relative keys. Minor often sounds darker.
A key signature at the start of a staff shows which notes are always sharp or flat. G major has one sharp, F♯; F major has one flat, B♭.
An interval is the distance between two notes. Count both notes: C to E is a third, C to G is a fifth, and C to the next C is an octave.
units.try: On a piano or keyboard app, play the C major scale, then the A natural minor scale. Sing along on “la.” Describe the difference in mood in one sentence each.
check: What is the step pattern of a major scale?
W W H W W W H
W H W W H W W
H W W W H W W
How many sharps does G major have?

learn: Harmony is two or more notes sounding together. A triad is a three-note chord built from a root, a third and a fifth. C major triad: C, E, G.
Chords can be named with Roman numerals by scale degree. In C major, I is C-E-G, IV is F-A-C and V is G-B-D. Uppercase numerals mean major and lowercase mean minor, such as vi (A-C-E).
Many songs use I, IV and V. The 12-bar blues uses them in a set order across 12 measures. The progression I–V–vi–IV appears in countless pop songs.
Consonance sounds stable and restful; dissonance sounds tense and wants to resolve. Composers use tension and release to create emotion.
units.try: Play or hum the root notes of the 12-bar blues in C: C C C C | F F C C | G F C C (one per measure). Clap four beats per measure as you go. Make up a simple lyric over it.
check: Which notes form a C major triad?
In C major, the V chord is built on

learn: Form is the structure of a piece. Binary form is AB, ternary is ABA, and rondo is ABACA, where a main theme keeps returning.
Theme and variations presents a melody and then changes it in rhythm, harmony or style. Popular songs often use verse, chorus and bridge.
Texture describes how layers combine. Monophonic is one melody alone; homophonic is melody with chords; polyphonic has two or more independent melodies at once, like a round.
A motive is a short musical idea, like the famous four-note opening of Beethoven’s Fifth Symphony, which is repeated and developed throughout a work.
units.try: Listen to a favorite song and map its form with letters or labels (intro, verse, chorus, bridge, outro). Note the time each section starts. Then sing a simple round with family to experience polyphony.
check: Melody with chord accompaniment is called

learn: Dynamics are volume levels: pp (pianissimo, very soft), p (piano, soft), mp, mf, f (forte, loud) and ff (fortissimo, very loud). Crescendo means gradually louder; decrescendo means gradually softer.
Articulation is how notes are attacked and connected: staccato is short and separated, legato is smooth and connected, and an accent stresses a note.
Timbre is tone color, the quality that makes a flute sound different from a trumpet playing the same pitch.
Instrument families: strings (violin, cello), woodwinds (flute, clarinet), brass (trumpet, tuba) and percussion (drums, xylophone). Voice types range from soprano and alto to tenor and bass.
units.try: Sing or hum “Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star” four ways: pianissimo and legato, then forte and staccato, then with a crescendo, then with accents on every first beat. Describe how each version changes the feeling.
check: The quality that makes instruments sound different on the same note is

learn: The Medieval and Renaissance periods (about 500 to 1600) featured chant and vocal polyphony. The Baroque period (1600 to 1750) brought ornate music by Bach, Handel and Vivaldi, with steady rhythms and harpsichord.
The Classical period (1750 to 1820) valued balance and clear form; Haydn, Mozart and early Beethoven wrote symphonies, sonatas and string quartets.
The Romantic period (1820 to 1900) emphasized emotion and larger orchestras; Chopin, Tchaikovsky and Verdi are examples.
The 20th and 21st centuries brought many styles, including Impressionism (Debussy), new rhythms (Stravinsky), minimalism (Philip Glass) and film scores.
units.try: Listen to a short Baroque piece (such as a Vivaldi concerto movement) and a Romantic piece (such as a Chopin nocturne). For each, write three words describing tempo, mood and instruments, and explain which period’s traits you heard.
check: Bach and Vivaldi belong to which period?
Which period emphasized emotion and larger orchestras?

learn: Spirituals were religious songs created by enslaved African Americans, carrying faith, sorrow and hope. They shaped later gospel music.

The blues began in the Deep South around 1900, using the 12-bar form and blue notes. Jazz grew in New Orleans in the early 1900s, featuring improvisation and swing; Louis Armstrong and Duke Ellington were leaders.
Country music grew from Appalachian folk and Southern traditions. Rock and roll in the 1950s blended rhythm and blues with country.
Hip-hop began in the Bronx, New York, in the 1970s, with DJs, rapping (MCing) and sampling. Latin styles like salsa and Tejano also enrich American music.
units.try: Make a timeline of five American music styles from spirituals to hip-hop. For each, write where and when it began and one musical feature. Listen to an example of one style you have never heard before.
check: Which style is known for improvisation and began in New Orleans?
The Bronx, New York, in the 1970s

learn: Every culture makes music. West African drumming often uses polyrhythms, where several different rhythms are layered, and call and response between a leader and group.
Indian classical music is built on ragas (melodic frameworks) and talas (rhythm cycles); the sitar and tabla are common instruments.
Indonesian gamelan ensembles use tuned metal gongs and xylophones that interlock patterns. Andean music from South America features panpipes and the charango.
Mexican mariachi uses violins, trumpets, guitars and the large guitarrón. Japanese music includes the koto, a 13-string zither.
units.try: Create a polyrhythm with a partner: one person taps 2 even beats per measure while the other taps 3, both starting together. Count slowly at first. Then try a call-and-response chant where you clap a pattern and the other person echoes it.
check: In Indian classical music, what is a raga?
An Indonesian ensemble of gongs and metal xylophones

learn: Composing starts with a small idea, such as a four-measure melody. Good melodies often move by step, include a few leaps, and end on the home note (tonic) to feel finished.
A phrase is a musical sentence, often four measures. A question phrase ends unresolved; an answer phrase ends on the tonic.
Lyrics should fit the rhythm, with stressed syllables on strong beats. Free notation apps or simple paper staves can record your ideas.

Performing well takes slow, focused practice. Practice tricky parts in small sections, use a metronome, breathe, and remember that mistakes are part of learning. Good audiences listen quietly and applaud at the end.
units.try: Compose an eight-measure melody in C major in 4/4 time: a four-measure question phrase that ends on G and a four-measure answer that ends on C. Write it with letter names and rhythms, then sing or play it for someone.
check: What is the tonic of a key?
The home note the scale is named for
The last note of every measure
A helpful way to practice a hard passage is to
Practice it slowly in small sections
Only play the whole piece fast

rooms.about: This course helps you build lifelong fitness and health habits: fitness components, safe training, nutrition, sleep, mental and emotional health, healthy relationships, substance-use risks, safety and first aid, and team and individual activities.

learn: Health-related fitness has five parts: cardiorespiratory endurance (heart and lungs), muscular strength, muscular endurance, flexibility and body composition.
Skill-related fitness includes agility, balance, coordination, power, reaction time and speed. These help in sports but are not required for good health.
Experts recommend that teens get at least 60 minutes of physical activity every day, mostly moderate to vigorous, with muscle- and bone-strengthening activities at least three days a week.
Fitness tests, like the PACER shuttle run or a sit-and-reach, measure your starting point. The goal is to compare with your own past results, not with others.
units.try: Check your baseline safely: count how many push-ups (or knee push-ups) you can do with good form, how long you can hold a plank, and how far you can reach in a seated toe touch. Write the numbers down and retest in four weeks.
check: How much physical activity should teens get each day?
Which is a health-related fitness component?

learn: The FITT principle guides training: Frequency (how often), Intensity (how hard), Time (how long) and Type (what activity). Change one part at a time to make progress.

Every workout should start with a 5 to 10 minute warm-up, such as light jogging and dynamic stretches like arm circles and leg swings, and end with a cool-down and static stretches held 15 to 30 seconds.
Find your pulse at the wrist or neck and count beats for 15 seconds, then multiply by 4 to get beats per minute. An estimated maximum heart rate is 220 minus your age.
Overload means gradually doing a bit more than your body is used to. Rest days let muscles recover. Sharp pain, dizziness or trouble breathing are signs to stop and tell an adult.
units.try: Design a 30-minute workout using FITT: 5-minute warm-up, 20 minutes of activity such as brisk walking, jumping jacks and squats, and a 5-minute cool-down with stretches. Check your pulse at rest and right after the main activity.
check: In the FITT principle, what does the I stand for?
What is the estimated maximum heart rate for a 14-year-old?

learn: The five food groups are fruits, vegetables, grains, protein foods and dairy (or fortified alternatives). Filling half your plate with fruits and vegetables is a helpful guide.
Nutrients include carbohydrates (main energy source), proteins (build and repair tissue), fats (energy and cell health), vitamins, minerals and water.
Read Nutrition Facts labels: check serving size first, then calories, added sugars, sodium and fiber. A % Daily Value of 5% or less is low; 20% or more is high.
Drink water throughout the day, especially during exercise. Limit sugary drinks; a single 20-ounce soda can contain more than 60 grams of sugar.
units.try: Look at the Nutrition Facts labels on two snacks at home. For each, write the serving size, calories, added sugar and %DV for fiber. Decide which is the better everyday choice and explain using the 5%/20% guide.
check: What should you check first on a Nutrition Facts label?
Which nutrient is the body’s main energy source?

learn: Teens need about 8 to 10 hours of sleep each night. Good sleep habits include a regular bedtime, a dark, cool room, and putting screens away about an hour before sleep.

Stress is the body’s response to challenges. Some stress can motivate you, but long-lasting stress can affect sleep, mood and health. Healthy coping includes exercise, deep breathing, talking to someone and breaking big tasks into steps.
Mental health is as important as physical health. It is normal to feel sad or worried sometimes, but feelings that last more than two weeks or get in the way of daily life are worth talking about.
Trusted adults include parents, school counselors, teachers, coaches and doctors. In the U.S., calling or texting 988 reaches a crisis line any time of day.
units.try: Practice box breathing: breathe in for 4 counts, hold for 4, breathe out for 4, hold for 4. Repeat four times. Then list three trusted adults you could talk to if you were feeling stressed or down.
check: How many hours of sleep do teens generally need?
Which is a healthy way to cope with stress?

learn: Healthy relationships, with friends, family or others, are built on respect, trust, honesty and good communication. Each person feels safe being themselves.
Warning signs of unhealthy relationships include controlling behavior, constant put-downs, pressure to do things you don’t want to do, and jealousy that limits who you can see.

Use I-messages to share feelings without blaming: “I feel upset when plans change last minute because I was looking forward to it.” Active listening means paying attention, nodding and repeating back what you heard.
Refusal skills help with peer pressure: say no clearly, give a reason, suggest something else, or leave. Everyone has the right to set boundaries about their body and personal space.
units.try: Write two I-messages for situations, such as a friend borrowing something without asking. Then role-play saying no to a dare with a family member using a clear no, a reason and an alternative activity.
check: I feel frustrated when I’m interrupted
Which is a warning sign of an unhealthy relationship?
One person controls who the other can see
Both people listen to each other

learn: Tobacco and nicotine, including vaping, are highly addictive. Nicotine can harm the developing teen brain, which keeps growing until about age 25.
Alcohol slows the brain and body, impairing judgment, coordination and reaction time. It is illegal for people under 21 in the United States.
Medicines are safe only when used as directed. Taking someone else’s prescription or taking more than directed can be dangerous.
Most teens do not use alcohol, tobacco or other drugs. Knowing the facts, having refusal skills and choosing friends who respect your decisions all help you stay healthy.
units.try: Make a pocket card with three ways to refuse an offer of vaping, such as “No thanks, I’ve got practice,” and three activities you enjoy instead. Practice saying them in a calm, confident voice.
check: What is the legal drinking age in the United States?
Why is nicotine especially harmful to teens?
It is addictive and can harm the developing brain
It has no effects on teens

learn: In an emergency, check the scene for danger, call 911 (or have someone call), and care for the person until help arrives. Do not move someone with a possible neck or back injury.
